title: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: t(1/r + 1/r') = C within each cavity of the heart

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: that is to say, that the thickness (_t_) of the wall varies inversely as the mean curvature.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XV, “On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures”; topic “Wall thickness of the heart”. Scope: heart chambers of mammals

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: t(1/r + 1/r') = C within each cavity of the heart

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch15-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The equation maps cleanly to imaging variables and can be tested with standard segmentation and surface analysis. Existing data permit a strong human test but do not match the full mammalian scope or uniform-pressure assumption.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From segmented cardiac images, calculate local principal curvatures and wall thickness within each chamber, then test whether thickness times mean curvature is constant and whether the apex is thinnest.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wall thickness varies with cardiac phase and loading.

Most open cohorts emphasize humans rather than mammals broadly.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.93
discriminating power: 0.78
data adequacy: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.72
data existence: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The inverse-curvature formula is explicit and cardiac MRI contours already support the regression in humans. That covers one mammal in detail and leaves the comparative scope thin. Partial-volume effects at the apex and the choice of which tissue counts as wall keep the test informative with a serious measurement confound.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From segmented cardiac surfaces, compute local wall thickness and mean curvature and test whether their product is constant within each chamber, with the left-ventricular apex the thinnest region. A flat thickness-curvature relation, or an apex as thick as the mid-wall, would refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trabeculae, papillary muscles and the phase of the cardiac cycle change both thickness and curvature.

Open segmentations are dominated by the human left ventricle and under-sample the right ventricle, atria and other mammals.
